title: How to Read a Landscape Contractor Quote (Line by Line)
seoTitle: How to Read a Landscape Quote – Line by Line
seoDescription: A landscape quote should have at least 6–8 line items. Here's what each one means and the red flags to check before you sign.
tldr: A well-prepared landscape quote breaks excavation, base prep, materials, labour, and disposal into separate line items — at minimum 6–8 distinct entries. Generic quotes with one or two lines often leave out crucial specs like base material type, paver product names, or excavation depth, which opens the door to change orders later. This guide walks you through every section of a typical Ontario hardscape quote so you can compare estimates fairly and know exactly what you're buying.
intro:
Getting three quotes is standard advice for any significant home project, but comparing landscaping quotes can be genuinely confusing if you don't know what the line items mean. A single number at the bottom of a page tells you very little about what the contractor is planning to actually build.

The structure of a quote — not just the total — reveals a great deal about how a contractor approaches their work. Contractors who itemise base prep, paver specs, and disposal separately have typically done enough projects in Barrie clay soil and Simcoe County freeze-thaw conditions to know exactly what goes wrong when any one of those elements is skimped on.

This guide walks through each section of a typical Ontario hardscape or outdoor-living quote: what it should say, what a vague or missing line often signals, and how to use the line items to do a fair apples-to-apples comparison when two numbers look very different.

sections.heading: Why the Structure of a Quote Matters as Much as the Total
sections.html:
A well-structured quote is a written description of the job. When a contractor lists 8–12 specific line items, they've essentially described their build method in dollar terms. When a quote lists two or three items — say, "landscaping" and "materials" — it's impossible to know what base depth they're assuming, which products they've spec'd, or whether disposal of excavated soil is included.

That gap matters most when things change on site. Ontario One Call is mandatory before any digging in Ontario, and soil conditions vary significantly across Simcoe County. Barrie clay-heavy lots behave differently from the sandy or moraine-influenced soils further north toward Oro-Medonte or Springwater. If the quote doesn't specify how the contractor handles unexpected conditions — rock, buried debris, saturated subgrade — there's no reference point when a change-order conversation arises.

At minimum, look for these 6 categories in any hardscape quote: (1) excavation and grading, (2) base material and preparation, (3) pavers or decking product with specs, (4) labour by task or phase, (5) edge restraints and drainage accessories, and (6) waste disposal and site cleanup. Quotes that consolidate these into fewer than 4 lines are almost always missing something that will affect either quality or final cost.

This doesn't mean every contractor writes an identical quote. Some bundle related tasks — that's fine as long as each bundle is described in enough detail that you understand what's included. A line reading "excavation, haul-off, and grading to finished grade" is a bundle — it still tells you disposal is included and that there's a grading step. That's very different from a line that simply reads "site prep."

sections.heading: The Excavation and Base Prep Line: The Most Important Section
sections.html:
Base preparation is where durable interlocking and cheap interlocking diverge most sharply. The finished surface looks identical at day one; the difference shows up after 3–5 Ontario winters. A proper base under a patio includes 3/4" clear stone over geotextile fabric, with an HPB (High Performance Bedding) layer for the final bedding course before the pavers set. The overall base depth is project-specific — soil type, intended load, and site drainage all affect it — which is why any quote that claims a single universal depth for all projects should prompt a follow-up question.

What to look for: excavation listed with a target depth relative to finished grade, identification of base material (3/4" clear stone, Granular A, HPB), and a note on how excavated material is handled — either haul-off included or a disposal allowance. Plate compaction passes should be mentioned; skipping them is a leading cause of paver settlement and joint sand loss.

Red flags: "base prep included" with no further detail. This phrase can mean almost anything — from a full engineered base to 50mm of screenings over native soil. If a quote's base section is vague, ask the contractor to specify material type, depth from subgrade to bedding layer, and compaction method. Their willingness to answer in writing tells you a great deal about how they run jobs.

Also check whether the quote includes anything for drainage. A 2% minimum slope spec, a catch basin, or swale grading notes signal that the contractor has thought about where water goes after installation. On Barrie's clay soils, water has nowhere to go without deliberate drainage design, and a patio that pools after rain will fail faster regardless of how solid the base is.

sections.heading: Materials: What “Pavers” and “Decking” Should Actually Specify
sections.html:
The materials line is where the most cost variation lives between competing quotes, and it's often the hardest to compare because contractors don't always disclose the specific product they're planning to use. A quote that says "pavers" without a product name and thickness is quoting you on a placeholder — the actual material could be anything from an 80mm Unilock Beacon Hill Smooth to a thinner imported product with no published performance data for Ontario freeze-thaw cycles.

For interlocking stone, the quote should name the manufacturer (Unilock, Techo-Bloc, or Permacon are the three brands we install), the product series, the thickness in mm, and the colour or finish. These specs drive material cost directly: Techo-Bloc Blu 80mm in a premium finish runs considerably more per square foot than a standard Permacon Flagstone in a comparable colour. If two quotes both say "pavers," you have no honest basis for comparison.

For composite decking, quotes should reference the product line and collection. TimberTech's Prime+ and Terrain collections have different surface textures, board widths, and pricing points. Fastening method — hidden clip system versus face screw — affects both labour time and the finished appearance of the deck, and should be specified.

Also check the edge restraint and accessory line. Properly pinned plastic or steel edge restraint, polymeric sand type (standard, permeable, or EnviroSand), and any step-nosing or soldier-course work should all appear as separate items. Edge restraint failure is a leading cause of paver migration over time, and the wrong polymeric sand in a heavily shaded or moist area can lose integrity within 2–3 seasons.

sections.heading: Labour and Equipment: How Ontario Contractors Typically Price It
sections.html:
Most landscape contractors in Ontario quote labour as a job total rather than an hourly rate — you won't typically see "20 hours at $X/hour." What you should see is some indication of which labour-intensive tasks are included and what equipment the crew will be using.

Equipment matters for two reasons: access and cost. A skid-steer loader on a constrained Barrie suburban lot will sometimes be replaced by a mini-excavator, which is slower and more expensive per cubic metre moved. If your backyard gate is under 36 inches wide, excavation often becomes fully hand-dig, which can add 20–40% to the excavation cost on a typical patio project. Detailed quotes flag access constraints and either adjust the scope accordingly or note a surcharge if conditions differ from those observed at the site visit.

Saw-cutting should be called out explicitly for patios with complex patterns or soldier-course borders. Wet-saw cutting on natural stone or porcelain adds meaningful labour time and blade wear — a quote that lumps all cutting into a general "installation" line may be assuming simpler patterns than you've discussed.

Disposal is frequently underestimated. A typical 500 sq ft interlocking patio generates roughly 15–25 tonnes of excavated material depending on depth and soil density — that's 2–3 truckloads to a licensed facility in the Barrie area. Quotes that include "haul-off" without specifying a tonnage allowance or confirming unlimited disposal can generate change orders if the job runs deeper than anticipated at quote time.

sections.heading: Allowances, Contingencies, and What Happens When Something Changes
sections.html:
An "allowance" in a quote is a placeholder amount for a cost that can't be pinned down without more information at the time of quoting. For example, a quote might carry a budgeted allowance for buried utility relocation if services are found in the work area. Allowances are legitimate and often appropriate; the question is whether they're realistic and clearly described. Ask the contractor how often their allowance estimates hold and what the adjustment process looks like.

A contingency line is similar but more general — a percentage buffer (commonly 5–15%) for unforeseen conditions. Not all quotes include one, and not including a contingency isn't a red flag on its own. What matters is how the quote addresses what happens when something unexpected turns up: is there a change-order process described, and is there a clause limiting change-order markups to a defined percentage above cost?

When reviewing any quote, look for language describing the change-order trigger and pricing method. The most contractor-friendly version charges time-and-materials at market rates with no cap; the most client-friendly version requires written sign-off before any out-of-scope work begins, with quoted unit rates for common additions. Reasonable quotes fall somewhere in the middle — typically requiring written approval and providing rates for the most likely additions, such as extra excavation per cubic metre or additional base material per tonne.

In Simcoe County, the most common change-order triggers on hardscape jobs are: buried debris or old foundations (common on infill lots in Barrie's south end and inner neighbourhoods), unexpectedly saturated soil requiring additional drainage work, and utility conflicts found after Ontario One Call marks were placed where actual depths differ from estimates. Knowing these risks before you sign is exactly what a detailed quote makes possible.

sections.heading: Payment Terms: What a Schedule Tells You About a Contractor
sections.html:
Payment terms are the last major section to review in any landscape quote, and they're often glossed over. A standard payment structure in Ontario landscape construction includes a deposit on signing, a progress payment when materials are delivered or at a defined project milestone, and a balance on completion. The exact percentages vary by contractor and project size, but a deposit in the range of 25–50% is typical for projects that require custom-ordered pavers or decking materials.

Red flags on the payment side: a request for 100% payment before work begins is outside normal practice for established contractors and limits your ability to ensure the job is finished to spec. Conversely, a quote with no deposit at all may signal that the contractor doesn't have a stable materials supply relationship — which can cause scheduling delays when material allocations aren't reserved. Ontario's consumer protection legislation gives homeowners specific rights around written contracts above a certain threshold, so it's worth knowing what documentation you should expect.

On larger projects, a 10% holdback held until 45 days after substantial completion is standard practice across Ontario's construction sector, providing meaningful protection against deficiencies. Smaller residential projects don't always use a formal holdback, but a final walkthrough step before the last payment is released is a reasonable ask on any project of meaningful scope.

When you're ready to compare estimates or simply want to understand a quote you've already received, our guide to choosing a landscaping contractor and our guide to hidden landscaping costs cover the selection and risk sides in depth. Our cost estimator is also useful for sanity-checking whether a total is in the right ballpark before you start collecting bids.

faqs.question: How many line items should a landscape quote have?
faqs.answer: A thorough hardscape quote typically has 8–12 line items covering excavation, base prep, materials with product specs, labour by phase, edge restraints and accessories, disposal, and payment terms. Fewer than 4 line items on any project of real complexity usually means multiple items have been bundled without enough description to verify what's included.

faqs.question: What does an 'allowance' mean in a landscaping quote?
faqs.answer: An allowance is a placeholder amount for a cost the contractor can't confirm until work begins — for example, a utility-relocation allowance if buried services are found in the work area. If the actual cost comes in lower, you typically receive credit; if higher, you pay the difference. Ask how often their allowance estimates hold and what the adjustment process looks like.

faqs.question: Should excavation depth be listed in the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes — but it should be framed as a target depth relative to finished grade rather than a fixed universal number. Base depth is project-specific in Ontario because Barrie clay soils behave very differently from the sandy or moraine-influenced soils further north in Simcoe County. What matters is that the contractor can explain their depth rationale when asked.

faqs.question: How do I compare two quotes with very different totals?
faqs.answer: Start with the base spec: same base material, same paver product, same disposal scope. Then check whether edge restraint and polymeric sand are itemised in both, and whether the labour scope covers the same tasks. Quotes missing any one of these can appear cheaper while planning a thinner, less durable build — the savings don't survive the first few Ontario winters.

faqs.question: Is a lump-sum quote acceptable?
faqs.answer: A lump-sum quote can work for very small, straightforward jobs. For anything involving excavation, custom-ordered materials, or more than a few days of work, a lump-sum with no line-item breakdown makes scope verification and fair comparison nearly impossible. It also gives you little basis for discussion if a change-order dispute arises mid-project.

faqs.question: What payment schedule is normal for landscape projects in Ontario?
faqs.answer: A typical structure involves a deposit of 25–50% at signing, a progress payment when materials are delivered or at a defined milestone, and the balance on completion after a walkthrough. A request for 100% payment before work begins is outside the norm for established contractors and reduces your ability to ensure the job is finished to spec.

faqs.question: What are the most common change-order triggers in Simcoe County?
faqs.answer: The three most common triggers we see on Barrie and Simcoe County hardscape jobs are: buried debris or old foundations uncovered during excavation, soil conditions significantly worse than the surface indicated (saturated clay requiring added drainage work), and utility conflicts after Ontario One Call marking where actual depths differ from initial estimates.

author_bio: Yorkis Estevez is Founder & Lead Builder of Golden Maple Landscaping, a Barrie-based hardscape and outdoor-living contractor working across Simcoe County. He focuses on interlocking stone, retaining walls, and composite decking, and spends a significant part of each client relationship helping people understand what a quote actually says before any work begins.
